name: Terminus Watch

stars.name: Terminus Watch
stars.notes: Aging K-dwarf with slightly sub-solar metallicity. Stable output with no significant variability detected across decades of monitoring.

planets.name: Sentinel
planets.notes: Dense iron-nickel world with virtually no mantle remaining. Likely the stripped core of a larger protoplanet from the system's violent early history.

planets.name: Vigil
planets.notes: Arid world in the habitable zone with a thin but stable nitrogen-CO2 atmosphere. Extensive canyon systems carved by ancient water flow. Two small, irregular moons suggest captured debris.

planets.name: Rampart
planets.notes: Sub-Saturn gas giant with muted grey-brown banding. Its largest moon, Watchtower, has a thin nitrogen atmosphere and surface ice deposits.

planets.name: Forlorn
planets.notes: Distant ice world in a slightly inclined orbit, suggesting late gravitational capture. Surface of dark nitrogen ice with impact craters preserved for billions of years.

anomalies.name: Vigil Canyon Resonance
anomalies.notes: Survey probe audio sensors detected sustained low-frequency harmonic vibrations in Vigil's canyon network. The oscillations appear to be wind-driven but maintain precise harmonic ratios unusual for natural systems.

asteroid_belts.name: The Watch Belt
asteroid_belts.notes: Mixed-composition belt with distinct silicate and carbonaceous populations. Contains some water-ice bearing bodies that could serve as fuel sources.

faction_control.notes: Unclaimed. The Terminus Drift is sparsely explored, and Terminus Watch has drawn no territorial interest despite Vigil's marginal habitability.

history: Terminus Watch was cataloged by an automated long-range survey in 2499. Vigil's position in the habitable zone and spectroscopic hints of a nitrogen atmosphere prompted a follow-up probe mission in 2523.

The probe confirmed Vigil's thin atmosphere and extensive canyon systems but found no evidence of liquid surface water or biological activity. The planet was classified as a marginal terraforming candidate and filed accordingly.

The harmonic vibrations detected in Vigil's canyons were included as an appendix in the probe's telemetry report. The phenomenon has been cited in two academic papers on aeolian resonance but has not prompted further investigation.
description: Terminus Watch sits in the quiet depths of the Terminus Drift, an amber-orange star presiding over four worlds that span the spectrum from stripped core to frozen exile. The system's architecture tells a story of early violence — Sentinel's missing mantle, the captured irregular moons of Vigil, Forlorn's inclined orbit — followed by billions of years of stillness. Today, everything is settled and stable, the ancient chaos preserved only in orbital scars.

Vigil, the second planet, is the system's most notable body. It sits in the habitable zone with a thin atmosphere and the carved remains of ancient river canyons — evidence that water once flowed here before being lost to space or locked underground. It is not habitable now, and making it so would require centuries of terraforming effort that no one has reason to invest. But it stands as a reminder of how close a world can come to being alive without quite reaching it.

The canyon harmonics are Terminus Watch's small mystery. Wind moving through Vigil's equatorial canyon network produces sustained tones at precise harmonic intervals — a natural organ played by an atmosphere too thin to support life. Whether the canyon geometry that produces this effect is coincidental erosion or something more deliberate is a question that generates occasional academic interest and no funding. The wind plays on, unheard except in a survey probe's archived recordings.
